# Exercises - 10 Applications of the STFT

## 10 Applications of the STFT

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Applications_STFT.html

#### `apps-stft-overview-1` - difficulty 1; concepts: stft-applications

**Q.** Which application is NOT among those covered in the Applications-of-STFT chapter?

- (a) Cross-synthesis
- (b) FFT filter banks
- (c) Sines+noise+transients modeling
- (d) Lossless audio compression

Hint 1: Lossless coding is not on the list.

Hint 2: Read the introductory bullet list.

**Answer: (d).** The chapter covers F0 estimation, cross-synthesis, spectral envelope extraction, sinusoidal modeling, S+N and S+N+T, chirplet modeling, time-scale modification, and FFT filter banks - but not lossless compression.

## 10.1 Estimation from Spectral Peaks

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Fundamental_Frequency_Estimation_Spectral.html

#### `apps-f0-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: f0-estimation, linear-regression

**Q.** How does the suggested F0 estimator combine peak frequencies into an estimate?

- (a) Take the lowest peak
- (b) Histogram peak-frequency differences for a nominal F0, then refine via linear regression of f_k=k·F_0
- (c) Take the FFT of the FFT
- (d) Average all peak frequencies

Hint 1: Most-common harmonic spacing is the rough F0.

Hint 2: Slope of (k, f_k) is the refined F0.

**Answer: (b).** Spacing histogram gives the nominal harmonic interval; least-squares straight-line fit through (k, f_k) refines it - F0 = slope. Approximate maximum-likelihood when peaks come from harmonic partials.

## 10.1 Useful Preprocessing

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Useful_Preprocessing.html

#### `apps-prep-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: preprocessing, masking

**Q.** Why is masking-based peak rejection useful in spectral peak-finding for audio?

- (a) It speeds up the FFT
- (b) Small peaks near larger peaks are inaudible (masked); rejecting them avoids tracking peaks that won't matter perceptually
- (c) It removes noise from the signal
- (d) It improves frequency resolution

Hint 1: Masking is a perceptual effect.

Hint 2: Don't track inaudible peaks.

**Answer: (b).** The auditory system masks weak peaks near loud ones. Rejecting peaks below the masking threshold (plus threshold of hearing) focuses tracking on perceptually important components.

## 10.1 Getting Closer to Maximum Likelihood

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Getting_Closer_Maximum_Likelihood.html

#### `apps-mle-f0-1` - difficulty 3; concepts: harmonic-comb, f0-mle

**Q.** In the harmonic-comb refinement of F0, what is the role of the small constant ε in Σ log(|X(k F0)| + ε)?

- (a) Numerical convenience only
- (b) It prevents a single missing/null partial (e.g., comb-filter null) from making the product zero, while implicitly penalizing missing terms
- (c) It speeds up convergence
- (d) It is the noise floor exact value

Hint 1: Think about what happens at a missing partial.

Hint 2: Avoids divide-by-zero or log(0) catastrophe.

**Answer: (b).** Without ε, a single near-zero |X(kF_0)| (e.g., from a spectral null) collapses the product (or pushes the log-sum to -∞). Adding a small ε bounds the per-partial penalty.

## 10.2 Cross-Synthesis

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Cross_Synthesis.html

#### `apps-cross-1` - difficulty 1; concepts: cross-synthesis, vocoder

**Q.** What does cross-synthesis do?

- (a) Sums two signals
- (b) Impresses the spectral envelope of one sound onto the (flattened) spectrum of another
- (c) Converts mono to stereo
- (d) Removes noise

Hint 1: Modulator provides the envelope; carrier provides the detail.

Hint 2: Used in commercial vocoders.

**Answer: (b).** The 'modulator' (e.g., voice) provides the time-varying envelope; the 'carrier' (e.g., wind) provides the fine spectral detail with its own envelope divided out. Result: 'talking wind' style effects.

## 10.3 Spectral Envelope Extraction

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Spectral_Envelope_Extraction.html

#### `apps-env-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: spectral-envelope, cepstrum-vs-lp

**Q.** Two methods are presented for extracting a spectral envelope. Which describes them correctly?

- (a) Both are parametric
- (b) Cepstral windowing is nonparametric (lowpass-filter the log-magnitude spectrum); linear prediction is parametric (all-pole source-filter model)
- (c) Both use linear prediction
- (d) Only LP works

Hint 1: Nonparametric vs. parametric.

Hint 2: One uses log-magnitude, one uses an all-pole model.

**Answer: (b).** Cepstral method liftters the cepstrum - no model assumption. LP fits an all-pole filter - parametric source-filter model. Both target a smooth envelope above the harmonic peaks.

## 10.3.1 Cepstral Windowing

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Cepstral_Windowing.html

#### `apps-cepstral-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: cepstral-windowing, lifter

**Q.** In cepstral envelope extraction for periodic signals, what should the cepstral cutoff n_c be set to?

- (a) Half the FFT length
- (b) Below the period in samples - so the cepstral 'rahmonic' due to F0 is liftered out
- (c) Always n_c=10
- (d) Whatever maximizes resolution

Hint 1: Keep low-quefrency, drop F0-rate periodicity.

Hint 2: Cepstral peak appears at the period.

**Answer: (b).** The fundamental period appears as a peak in the cepstrum at index P. Truncating below P keeps formant structure (low-quefrency) but removes the harmonic comb (high-quefrency).

## 10.3.2 Linear Prediction Spectral Envelope

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Linear_Prediction_Spectral_Envelope.html

#### `lpc-ztransform-1` - difficulty 1; concepts: lpc, z-transform, all-pole-filter, source-filter

**Q.** A signal y(n) is predicted from M past samples: y(n) = −a_1 y(n−1) − … − a_M y(n−M) + e(n). Taking the z-transform, which expression correctly gives Y(z) in terms of the prediction-error transform E(z) and the monic predictor polynomial A(z) = 1 + a_1 z^(−1) + … + a_M z^(−M)?

- (a) Y(z) = E(z) / A(z)
- (b) Y(z) = A(z) · E(z)
- (c) Y(z) = E(z) − A(z)
- (d) Y(z) = 1 / [E(z) · A(z)]

Hint 1: Move all Y terms to the left side after taking z-transforms.

Hint 2: The delay identity: y(n−k) ↔ z^(−k) Y(z).

**Answer: (a).** Taking the z-transform of the prediction equation and collecting all Y(z) terms on the left gives A(z)Y(z) = E(z), so Y(z) = E(z)/A(z). The signal is the output of an all-pole filter 1/A(z) driven by the prediction error E(z). Option (b) would make A(z) the system response rather than its inverse.

#### `lpc-envelope-1` - difficulty 1; concepts: lpc, spectral-envelope, power-spectral-density, all-pole-filter

**Q.** After optimal LP analysis, the prediction error e(n) is whitened to variance σ_e^2. Which pair of expressions correctly gives the spectral magnitude envelope |Y(ω)| and power spectral density S_y(ω) of the output signal?

- (a) |Y(ω)| = σ_e / |A(ω)| and S_y(ω) = σ_e^2 / |A(ω)|^2
- (b) |Y(ω)| = σ_e^2 / |A(ω)| and S_y(ω) = σ_e / |A(ω)|^2
- (c) |Y(ω)| = |A(ω)| / σ_e and S_y(ω) = |A(ω)|^2 / σ_e^2
- (d) |Y(ω)| = σ_e · |A(ω)| and S_y(ω) = σ_e^2 · |A(ω)|^2

Hint 1: For a system H(ω) driven by white noise with variance σ^2, the output PSD is σ^2|H(ω)|^2.

Hint 2: Here H(ω) = 1/A(ω).

**Answer: (a).** From Y(z) = E(z)/A(z) and white noise error with PSD σ_e^2, the output PSD is S_y(ω) = σ_e^2/|A(ω)|^2. The spectral magnitude envelope is the square root: |Y(ω)| = σ_e/|A(ω)|. Options (c) and (d) have A in the numerator, which would make peaks in A become peaks in the output—the opposite of an all-pole filter.

## 10.3.2 Linear Prediction is Peak Sensitive

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Linear_Prediction_Peak_Sensitive.html

#### `lpc-peaks-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: lpc, peak-sensitivity, rayleigh-energy-theorem, spectral-envelope

**Q.** LP minimizes \(\|\hat{e}\|_2^2\). By Rayleigh's energy theorem this equals \(\frac{1}{2\pi}\int|\hat{A}(e^{j\omega})Y(e^{j\omega})|^2\,d\omega\). Rewriting as \(\frac{\hat{\sigma}_e^2}{2\pi}\int\left|\frac{Y(e^{j\omega})}{\hat{Y}(e^{j\omega})}\right|^2 d\omega\), what does this imply about how LP fits spectral peaks?

- (a) LP tends to overestimate spectral peaks, because the integrand is smallest when |Ŷ(ω)| > |Y(ω)|
- (b) LP tends to underestimate spectral peaks, because the integrand is smallest when |Ŷ(ω)| < |Y(ω)|
- (c) LP fits peaks and valleys equally, because the integral averages over all frequencies
- (d) LP overestimates valleys and underestimates peaks to minimize total energy

Hint 1: Look at the integrand |Y/Ŷ|^2: minimizing the integral means reducing the ratio where it is large, i.e., where Y has peaks.

Hint 2: Making |Ŷ| bigger than |Y| at a peak shrinks the ratio and reduces error.

**Answer: (a).** The ratio |Y|/|Ŷ| is smallest when |Ŷ| is large relative to |Y|, so the error integral is minimized by driving LP to make |Ŷ(ω)| > |Y(ω)| wherever possible—i.e., LP overestimates peaks. Since A(z) is constrained to be monic and minimum-phase, its log magnitude is zero-mean, so each peak overestimation is compensated by a valley underestimation of equal log-area.

## 10.3.2 Linear Prediction Methods

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Linear_Prediction_Methods.html

#### `apps-lp-methods-1` - difficulty 3; concepts: linear-prediction, autocorrelation-method, covariance-method

**Q.** What is the key difference between the autocorrelation and covariance methods of linear prediction?

- (a) Autocorrelation uses Bartlett-windowed (biased) autocorrelations and guarantees minimum-phase A(z); covariance uses unbiased autocorrelations - more accurate bandwidths but no stability guarantee
- (b) They are identical
- (c) Covariance is faster
- (d) Autocorrelation cannot be solved on a computer

Hint 1: Bias vs. variance trade-off.

Hint 2: Min-phase guarantee comes at the cost of accuracy.

**Answer: (a).** Autocorrelation method: implicit zero outside the frame (Bartlett bias); always min-phase, but overdamped formants. Covariance method: unbiased; sharper formants but possibly unstable. Burg/lattice methods balance the two.

## 10.3.2 Computation of Linear Prediction Coefficients

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Computation_Linear_Prediction_Coefficients.html

#### `apps-lpc-comp-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: lpc-normal-equations, durbin-recursion

**Q.** Why do the LP normal equations admit an O(M^2) Durbin recursion solution?

- (a) Because M is small
- (b) Because the autocorrelation matrix R is symmetric Toeplitz
- (c) Because the FFT computes them
- (d) Lucky coincidence

Hint 1: Toeplitz structure is exploited.

Hint 2: Levinson/Durbin recursion.

**Answer: (b).** Symmetric Toeplitz structure of R[i,j]=r(|i-j|) lets the Durbin recursion solve the system in O(M^2) instead of the O(M^3) cost of generic LU decomposition.

## 10.3.2 Linear Prediction Order Selection

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Linear_Prediction_Order_Selection.html

#### `lp-order-formants-1` - difficulty 1; concepts: linear-prediction, model-order, formants, spectral-envelope

**Q.** For computing a spectral envelope of voice by linear prediction, roughly how large should the predictor order M be?

- (a) Equal to the number of spectral formants
- (b) About twice the number of spectral formants, perhaps a little larger
- (c) About ten times the number of spectral formants
- (d) Equal to the number of samples in the analysis frame

Hint 1: Count how many model orders a single resonant peak costs.

Hint 2: A resonance needs a complex-conjugate pole pair — two orders each.

**Answer: (b).** Each resonance (formant) requires a complex-conjugate pole pair, i.e., two orders of the all-pole model, so M should be about twice the number of formants, plus a little extra to allow more detailed modeling of spectral shape away from the formants. One order per formant (a) cannot form a resonance; ten times (c) would make the envelope follow the spectral fine structure that does not belong in an envelope; the frame length (d) is unrelated to the order.

#### `lp-order-sinusoids-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: linear-prediction, model-order, spectral-envelope, sinusoids

**Q.** For a signal consisting of a sum of quasi sinusoids, how should the linear-prediction order M be chosen when the goal is a spectral envelope?

- (a) Significantly less than twice the number of sinusoids
- (b) Exactly twice the number of sinusoids
- (c) Significantly more than twice the number of sinusoids
- (d) Exactly the number of sinusoids plus one

Hint 1: Ask what happens if the model has enough poles to put one resonance on every partial.

Hint 2: You want too few poles to resolve individual sinusoids.

**Answer: (a).** Twice the number of sinusoids is exactly enough for the all-pole model to place a sharp resonance on each sinusoid, which would make the 'envelope' track the individual partials rather than their overall shape. Keeping M significantly below that value inhibits modeling the sinusoids as spectral-envelope peaks. Choices (b) and (c) supply enough (or more than enough) poles to model each sinusoid individually; (d) is not the criterion given.

## 10.3.2 Summary of LP Spectral Envelopes

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Summary_LP_Spectral_Envelopes.html

#### `apps-lp-summary-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: lp-envelope, source-filter

**Q.** How is the LP spectral envelope expressed?

- (a) g/A(z) the all-pole frequency response with prediction-error gain
- (b) The FFT of the autocorrelation
- (c) g · A(z)
- (d) log|X(ω)|

Hint 1: All-pole filter; gain is prediction-error rms.

Hint 2: Source-filter model.

**Answer: (a).** Ŷ_m(ω) = ĝ/|Â(e^(jω))|, where A is the LP polynomial and g is the rms residual amplitude. Driving 1/A by white noise reproduces a signal with this envelope.

## 10.3.3 Signal Synthesis

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Signal_Synthesis.html

#### `apps-signal-synth-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: source-filter-synthesis, vowel

**Q.** In the LP synthesis 'ah' example, why is the source signal a bandlimited impulse train (sum of cosines at harmonics of F0)?

- (a) It is the simplest
- (b) It models the periodic glottal excitation; convolving with the all-pole formant filter produces a vowel sound
- (c) Random choice
- (d) Only impulses can drive an IIR

Hint 1: Source = glottis; filter = vocal tract.

Hint 2: Impulse train models periodic glottal pulses.

**Answer: (b).** Source-filter speech model: glottal pulses (modeled by impulse train, here as bandlimited cosines) drive the vocal-tract resonances (modeled by the LP all-pole filter). Together they synthesize voiced speech.

## 10.3.3 Spectral Envelope by the Cepstral Windowing Method

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Spectral_Envelope_Cepstral_Windowing.html

#### `apps-cep-env-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: cepstral-windowing, smooth-lifter

**Q.** Why might Hann-windowing the cepstrum (instead of rectangular truncation) be preferable for spectral-envelope extraction?

- (a) Hann is always better
- (b) Smooth (Hann) lifter avoids the abrupt truncation artifacts that rectangular windows would produce in the smoothed spectrum
- (c) It is faster
- (d) Smaller memory

Hint 1: Sharp time-domain cuts cause ringing.

Hint 2: Same trade-off as in spectrum analysis windows.

**Answer: (b).** Rectangular cepstral truncation produces sinc-like ringing in the resulting log-magnitude spectrum. A graceful Hann-shape lifter yields smoother envelope curves while still removing F0 components.

## 10.3.3 Spectral Envelope by Linear Prediction

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Spectral_Envelope_Linear_Prediction.html

#### `apps-lp-env-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: lp-envelope-validation, model-match

**Q.** Why is the LP envelope expected to be exact for the synthetic 'ah' vowel example?

- (a) Numerical luck
- (b) The vowel was synthesized as an IIR all-pole filter with M=6 poles driven by a bandlimited impulse train, exactly matching the LP model
- (c) Hamming window
- (d) It is not exact

Hint 1: Synthesis model and LP model match exactly.

Hint 2: 6 poles for 3 formants.

**Answer: (b).** The synthesized vowel matches the LP signal model perfectly (3 formant pole pairs; the source is approximately white in the frequency band of interest). M=6 LP coefficients should recover the vocal-tract filter exactly.

## 10.3.3 Linear Prediction in Matlab and Octave

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Linear_Prediction_Matlab_Octave.html

#### `lp-burg-stability-1` - difficulty 1; concepts: linear-prediction, burg-method, minimum-phase, stability

**Q.** What advantage does Burg's method (the default in the Octave-Forge `lpc` function) have over the covariance method of linear prediction?

- (a) It requires no windowing of the data
- (b) It always produces a lower prediction error than the covariance method
- (c) It guarantees that A(z) is minimum phase, so the resulting synthesis filter is stable
- (d) It is the only method that can be computed with the FFT

Hint 1: The covariance method's weak point is not accuracy.

Hint 2: Think about whether the all-pole synthesis filter 1/A(z) is guaranteed usable.

**Answer: (c).** Burg's method guarantees stability — the prediction-error filter A(z) comes out minimum phase, so 1/A(z) is stable — while yielding accuracy comparable to the covariance method (which does not guarantee stability). Its accuracy is stated to be comparable, not superior, so (b) is wrong; (a) and (d) are not claimed anywhere.

## 10.4 Spectral Modeling Synthesis

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Spectral_Modeling_Synthesis.html

#### `sinmodel-fm-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: analytic-signal, hilbert-transform, fm-synthesis, single-sideband, sinusoidal-modeling

**Q.** To generate FM noise (a noise band whose center frequency is sinusoidally modulated), the bandpass-filtered noise must first be converted to an analytic signal before multiplying by the complex FM carrier. Why is this analytic-signal step necessary?

- (a) Without it, the real bandpass noise has both positive- and negative-frequency components, so complex modulation shifts both, producing two noise bands instead of one.
- (b) Without it, the bandpass filter cannot be applied after modulation.
- (c) Without it, the FM carrier frequency would be doubled.
- (d) Without it, the noise bandwidth B would be halved.

Hint 1: A real signal has a two-sided spectrum: components at both +f_c and −f_c.

Hint 2: Complex (single-sideband) modulation shifts all frequency content by the carrier frequency; starting from a two-sided signal produces two output bands.

**Answer: (a).** A real bandpass signal has mirror-image spectral content at ±f_c. Multiplying by e^{jφ(t)} shifts both the positive-frequency band (to f_c + f_m) and its negative-frequency mirror (to −f_c + f_m), yielding two distinct noise bands. Converting to an analytic signal first eliminates the negative-frequency mirror, so only one FM-modulated noise band appears after modulation.

## 10.4.1 Additive Synthesis (Early Sinusoidal Modeling)

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Additive_Synthesis_Early_Sinusoidal.html

#### `sinmodel-add-speech-1` - difficulty 1; concepts: additive-synthesis, sinusoidal-modeling, speech-intelligibility, partial-tracking

**Q.** When applying sinusoidal (additive) analysis-synthesis to a short speech utterance and tracking spectral peaks over time, roughly how many sinusoidal partials are needed to make the resynthesized speech intelligible?

- (a) Only 1 partial (the fundamental frequency)
- (b) 2–3 partials
- (c) 10–20 partials
- (d) At least 50 partials

Hint 1: Sine-wave speech demonstrations show that intelligibility survives with very few sinusoidal components.

Hint 2: Intelligibility and high-quality fidelity require very different numbers of components.

**Answer: (b).** Experiments with sinusoidal modeling of speech (e.g., the classic Remez et al. sine-wave speech work and corroborated by additive-synthesis assignments) show that tracking just 2–3 amplitude/frequency trajectories is sufficient for intelligibility. The auditory system reconstructs the phonetic content from a sparse set of resonance-like trajectories, even though a faithful perceptual reproduction requires far more components.

#### `sinmodel-add-speech-2` - difficulty 2; concepts: additive-synthesis, sinusoidal-modeling, speech-analysis, sines-plus-noise, partial-tracking

**Q.** Compared to sinusoidal modeling of a bird chirp, sinusoidal modeling of human speech is more difficult primarily because:

- (a) Speech is sampled at a lower rate than typical bird-song recordings.
- (b) Speech has a more complex spectrum requiring more sinusoidal components, and also contains noise and transient components that are not well modeled by sinusoids alone.
- (c) The fundamental frequency of speech is higher than that of a bird chirp, causing aliasing.
- (d) The window length required for speech analysis is much shorter than for bird-song analysis.

Hint 1: Think about what distinguishes voiced speech from a simple sinusoidal tone.

Hint 2: Fricatives and stop consonants are not well-modeled by slowly varying sinusoids.

**Answer: (b).** A bird chirp is quasi-sinusoidal with a small number of well-separated, trackable partials and a high SNR (~60 dB in the lab example). Human speech has a denser harmonic structure requiring many more sinusoids for quality reproduction, and it contains significant noise-like (fricatives, aspiration) and transient (stop consonants) components that violate the pure sinusoidal model.

#### `sinmodel-fm-2` - difficulty 1; concepts: instantaneous-frequency, phase-accumulation, fm-synthesis, discrete-integration, sinusoidal-modeling

**Q.** In FM noise generation, the complex carrier is defined as x_c[n] = e^{j · 2πT ∑_(k=0)^n x_m[k]}, where x_m[k] = A_m sin(2π f_m k T) is the modulation signal. Why is the *sum* (accumulation) of x_m[k] used rather than x_m[n] directly as the exponent?

- (a) The instantaneous frequency of the carrier equals the derivative of its phase; conversely, the instantaneous phase is the running integral (sum) of the instantaneous frequency over past samples.
- (b) Summation averages out noise in x_m[k], smoothing the carrier phase.
- (c) Summation ensures the carrier amplitude equals one at all times.
- (d) Summation converts the sinusoidal modulation to a square-wave modulation.

Hint 1: Phase is the integral of instantaneous frequency with respect to time.

Hint 2: In discrete time, integration becomes summation over past samples.

**Answer: (a).** Instantaneous frequency ω(n) = dθ/dn, so the phase θ(n) = ∑_(k=0)^n ω(k) · T. To make the carrier frequency follow x_m[n] at each sample, the phase must be the running sum (discrete-time integral) of x_m. Using x_m[n] directly as the exponent would give a phase that oscillates at f_m rather than a carrier whose frequency oscillates at f_m.

#### `sinmodel-phase-1` - difficulty 1; concepts: phase-accumulation, additive-synthesis, instantaneous-frequency, phase-continuity, sinusoidal-modeling

**Q.** An additive-synthesis inner loop uses the code fragment `output += a * sin(f * t + phases[i])` where `f` is updated linearly frame-to-frame and `t` is a sample counter reset to zero at each frame. What is wrong with this approach?

- (a) It does not accumulate phase across frames, so the phase at the start of each frame is reset to `phases[i]` rather than continuing from where the oscillator left off, causing discontinuities.
- (b) Linear interpolation of frequency is not possible; it must be exponential.
- (c) The amplitude `a` must be accumulated in the same way as phase.
- (d) The `sin` function is too slow; a table lookup must be used instead.

Hint 1: Think about what φ(t) = ∫_0^t ω(τ)dτ means: phase is the running integral of frequency.

Hint 2: If t is reset to zero every frame, the integral restarts at zero instead of continuing from its previous value.

**Answer: (a).** Resetting `t=0` at each frame and using `phases[i]` directly means the oscillator phase is not continuous across frame boundaries. Instantaneous frequency determines the *rate of phase change*, so the phase must be a running integral (accumulated sum) of the per-sample frequency values. Each frame must pick up from the phase value accumulated at the end of the previous frame; otherwise the sinusoid has artificial phase jumps at every frame boundary.

#### `sinmodel-phase-2` - difficulty 2; concepts: phase-accumulation, instantaneous-frequency, discrete-integration, additive-synthesis, oscillator-design

**Q.** In the correct additive-synthesis oscillator, the sample-by-sample phase update is θ[n] = θ[n−1] + ω[n]·T, where ω[n] is the instantaneous radian frequency and T is the sampling period. This differs from storing the frequency and multiplying by the sample index. Which fundamental relationship justifies using the recursive accumulation?

- (a) Instantaneous frequency is the derivative of phase with respect to time: ω(t) = dθ/dt, so θ(t) = ∫ω(t)dt, which in discrete time becomes θ[n] = θ[n−1] + ω[n]T.
- (b) The Nyquist theorem requires that phase be sampled at twice the frequency.
- (c) Multiplying by the sample index would give a constant frequency, not a time-varying one.
- (d) Phase must be bounded in [0, 2π), requiring a modular accumulator.

Hint 1: Phase is the time-integral of instantaneous frequency.

Hint 2: Discrete-time integration is a running (recursive) sum, not a product of frequency and sample index.

**Answer: (a).** By definition, instantaneous frequency ω(t) = dθ(t)/dt. Integrating both sides: θ(t) = θ(0) + ∫_0^t ω(τ)dτ. In discrete time with sample period T, the integral becomes a sum: θ[n] = θ[0] + T∑_(k=1)^nω[k], or equivalently θ[n] = θ[n−1] + ω[n]T. This recursive accumulation ensures phase continuity and correct instantaneous frequency at every sample.

#### `apps-additive-1` - difficulty 1; concepts: additive-synthesis, envelopes

**Q.** How is a signal represented in additive synthesis (early sinusoidal modeling)?

- (a) Sum of A_i(t) sin(θ_i(t)) - sinusoids each with independent slowly-varying amplitude and phase
- (b) A single oscillator with FM
- (c) Filtered noise
- (d) A delay line

Hint 1: Each partial has its own envelopes.

Hint 2: Generalizes wavetable to independent partials.

**Answer: (a).** Additive synthesis sums many partials, each with its own A(t) and frequency envelope. Envelopes typically come from STFT analysis at a low frame rate.

## 10.4.2 Additive Synthesis Analysis

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Additive_Synthesis_Analysis.html

#### `addsyn-phase-transient-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: additive-synthesis, phase, attack-transient, sinusoidal-modeling

**Q.** In additive-synthesis analysis, why is the measured phase of each sinusoidal peak needed for frames containing an attack transient, but generally not for steady-state frames?

- (a) Phase measurements are only accurate during transients
- (b) Phase is not perceived in steady-state tones, but it controls the position of time-domain features within a frame
- (c) The amplitude and frequency trajectories are undefined during a transient
- (d) Steady-state frames have zero phase by definition

Hint 1: Think about what a listener can and cannot hear.

Hint 2: Phase alignment across partials determines the shape and timing of the waveform within the frame.

**Answer: (b).** Phase is normally not perceived in steady-state tones, so it may be discarded there. During an attack transient or any other abrupt change, however, the relative phases of the sinusoidal peaks determine where the time-domain features (such as the attack itself) sit inside the analysis frame, so phase must be retained. (a) is backwards; (c) and (d) are simply false.

## 10.4.2 Following Spectral Peaks

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Following_Spectral_Peaks.html

#### `apps-track-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: frame-rate, envelope-sampling

**Q.** What is the typical frame rate for sinusoidal-modeling analysis envelopes in speech?

- (a) 44 kHz
- (b) 200 Hz (5 ms hop) - much lower than the audio sample rate, allowing dramatic data reduction
- (c) 1 Hz
- (d) Same as audio sample rate

Hint 1: Envelopes vary slowly compared to audio.

Hint 2: 5 ms is the conventional speech-analysis hop.

**Answer: (b).** 5 ms hop = 200 Hz envelope rate is typical for speech. The envelopes are then upsampled (linearly interpolated) to the audio rate at synthesis time - hundreds-fold compression.

## 10.4.2 Sinusoidal Peak Finding

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Sinusoidal_Peak_Finding.html

#### `sinespec-peak-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: peak-amplitude, windowed-sinusoid, dc-gain

**Q.** For a windowed complex sinusoid with complex amplitude A_x and frequency ω_x, what is the DTFT magnitude at the peak?

- (a) |X_w(ω_x)| = |A_x| × M
- (b) |X_w(ω_x)| = |A_x| × |W(0)|
- (c) |X_w(ω_x)| = |W(ω_x)|
- (d) |X_w(ω_x)| = |A_x|^2

Hint 1: The windowed sinusoid's spectrum is A_x W(ω-ω_x).

Hint 2: At ω = ω_x, we evaluate W(0).

**Answer: (b).** At the sinusoid frequency ω_x, the DTFT magnitude equals |A_x| × |W(0)|, where W(0) is the window transform at DC. If the window is scaled to have unity DC gain (W(0)=1), the peak magnitude equals the sinusoid amplitude |A_x|.

#### `sinespec-peak-2` - difficulty 2; concepts: zero-phase-window, phase-estimation, spectral-peak

**Q.** If we use a zero-phase (even) window, what is the relationship between the phase at the spectral peak and the sinusoid's phase?

- (a) They differ by π/2
- (b) They are equal
- (c) They differ by π
- (d) There is no relationship

Hint 1: A zero-phase window has a real Fourier transform in the main lobe.

Hint 2: Since W(0) is real and positive, it contributes zero phase.

**Answer: (b).** For a zero-phase (even) window, W(0) is real and positive, so the phase at the spectral peak equals the phase of the sinusoid: angle(X_w(ω_x)) = angle(A_x).

## 10.4.2 Tracking Sinusoidal Peaks in a Sequence of FFTs

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Tracking_Sinusoidal_Peaks_Sequence.html

#### `apps-track-seq-1` - difficulty 1; concepts: peak-tracking, afp-triple

**Q.** What three quantities does sinusoidal-peak tracking record per peak per frame?

- (a) Amplitude, frequency, phase
- (b) Amplitude, bandwidth, decay
- (c) Cepstrum, autocorrelation, group delay
- (d) FFT bin index only

Hint 1: Same triple as PARSHL.

Hint 2: Phase can be discarded for steady tones.

**Answer: (a).** Standard analysis tracks (amplitude, frequency, phase) of each peak across frames. Quadratic interpolation is used to refine spectral magnitude peaks. Phase is sometimes optional.

## 10.4.3 Sines + Noise Modeling

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Sines_Noise_Modeling.html

#### `apps-sn-modeling-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: sines-noise-modeling

**Q.** Why does S+N modeling add a filtered-noise component to additive synthesis?

- (a) To increase compression
- (b) Synthesizing noise faithfully would require many sinusoids per critical band - filtered noise (subtractive synthesis) handles this efficiently
- (c) It is required by the FFT
- (d) To reduce CPU

Hint 1: Sinusoids are inefficient at modeling noise.

Hint 2: Add subtractive synthesis.

**Answer: (b).** Up to ~25 sinusoids per critical band would be needed to mimic noise reliably - far too costly. S+N adds a stochastic component (white noise filtered by a slowly-varying envelope), letting sinusoids handle just the tonal peaks.

## 10.4.3 Sines+Noise Analysis

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Sines_Noise_Analysis.html

#### `apps-sn-analysis-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: sn-analysis, residual-spectrum

**Q.** How is the residual ('noise') spectrum obtained in S+N analysis?

- (a) Random sampling
- (b) By subtracting the magnitude spectrum of the resynthesized sinusoids from the original STFT magnitude spectrum
- (c) Hamming-window the input
- (d) Compute the autocorrelation

Hint 1: Resynthesize sines, FFT, subtract magnitude.

Hint 2: Envelope-fit the residual.

**Answer: (b).** Tracked sinusoids are resynthesized, windowed, and FFT'd. Their magnitude spectrum is subtracted from the original to leave the noise residual; an upper envelope is then fit to it.

## 10.4.3 S+N Synthesis

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/S_N_Synthesis.html

#### `apps-sn-synth-1` - difficulty 3; concepts: filtered-noise-synthesis, random-phase

**Q.** How is filtered white noise synthesized efficiently in the frequency domain in S+N synthesis?

- (a) Multiply the spectral envelope by random unit-modulus phases (uniform on [-π,π)) - the IFFT yields approximately Gaussian noise (CLT)
- (b) Just add Gaussian noise
- (c) Use white noise directly
- (d) Apply a Hann window

Hint 1: Random phase is the trick.

Hint 2: Central limit theorem gives Gaussian samples.

**Answer: (a).** Random phase × envelope → IFFT produces filtered noise; CLT makes it approximately Gaussian. Use 50% overlap and a non-rectangular window to handle changing envelope without artifacts.

## 10.4.3 Sines+Noise Summary

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Sines_Noise_Summary.html

#### `apps-sn-summary-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: sn-tsm

**Q.** Why is S+N modeling well suited for time-scale modification?

- (a) Lower bit rate
- (b) The model consists entirely of slowly-varying envelopes (plus optional transient phase) - resampling them in time slows or speeds the audio without distorting pitch or formants
- (c) Because noise is fast
- (d) It is not suited for TSM

Hint 1: Envelopes are easy to time-warp.

Hint 2: Same idea as in PARSHL.

**Answer: (b).** Envelopes can be linearly interpolated/resampled in time without changing their per-frame frequency content. Phase needs special handling at transients.

## 10.4.4 Sines + Noise + Transients Models

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Sines_Noise.html

#### `apps-snt-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: snt, transient-model

**Q.** Why are transients handled separately in sines+noise+transients (S+N+T) modeling?

- (a) Transients are noisy
- (b) Sinusoids and stationary noise are inefficient at modeling sharp time-domain events; transients need a dedicated model (e.g., wavelet, frequency-domain LPC, or AAC interval)
- (c) Transients are inaudible
- (d) Transients are removed before processing

Hint 1: Localized in time = wideband in frequency.

Hint 2: Sines are bad at sudden onsets.

**Answer: (b).** A wideband transient would demand many sines to reproduce. A separate transient model (or intact-AAC interval) preserves crispness without pollution of the steady-state model.

## 10.4.4 Sines+Noise+Transients Time-Frequency Maps

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Sines_Noise_Transients_Time_Frequency_Maps.html

#### `apps-snt-tf-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: snt-time-frequency-map, noise-substitution

**Q.** In the original S+N+T system, what is done with frequencies above 5 kHz between transients?

- (a) Discarded
- (b) Amplitude-modulated noise substitution (no sinusoids tracked)
- (c) Sinusoids only
- (d) Transient model

Hint 1: Critical bands are wide at high frequencies.

Hint 2: Noise substitution suffices for high-frequency content.

**Answer: (b).** Above ~5 kHz between transients, the system uses noise substitution because sines are inefficient and the ear has wider critical bands at high frequencies, making the substitution inaudible.

## 10.4.4 Sines+Noise+Transients Noise Model

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Sines_Noise_Transients_Noise_Model.html

#### `snt-bark-noise-gain-1` - difficulty 1; concepts: sines-noise-transients, bark-bands, noise-modeling, spectral-envelope

**Q.** In the Sines+Noise+Transients noise model illustrated in the text, what determines the noise gain used in a given band at a given frame time?

- (a) The peak magnitude of the largest sinusoid in that band
- (b) The phase variance of the bins in that band
- (c) The summed energy in that Bark band for that frame
- (d) The zero-crossing rate of the residual in that band

Hint 1: The bands are Bark bands — one gain per band per frame.

Hint 2: It is an energy measurement, summed over the band.

**Answer: (c).** The energy in each Bark band is summed, and that sum is used as the gain for the noise in that band at that frame time. Sinusoidal peak magnitude (a) belongs to the sinusoidal model, not the noise model; phase variance (b) and zero-crossing rate (d) play no role in this gain computation.

#### `snt-bark-stepsize-1` - difficulty 1; concepts: sines-noise-transients, bark-bands, amplitude-envelope, time-resolution

**Q.** For the Bark bands above 5 kHz in this noise model, approximately what step size is used for the piecewise-linear noise amplitude envelope?

- (a) 0.3 ms
- (b) 3 ms
- (c) 30 ms
- (d) 300 ms

Hint 1: High-frequency Bark bands are wide, so their envelopes must be sampled quickly.

Hint 2: It is a single-digit number of milliseconds.

**Answer: (b).** The text states that the step size for all Bark bands above 5 kHz is approximately 3 ms. Such a short step is needed because high-frequency bands are wide, so their envelopes can change quickly. 0.3 ms (a) would be far finer than needed, while 30 ms (c) and 300 ms (d) would smear transients badly.

## 10.5 Time Scale Modification

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Time_Scale_Modification.html

#### `sinmodel-vocoder-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: instantaneous-amplitude, beating, phase-vocoder, two-sinusoid-model, complex-sinusoid

**Q.** In the phase-vocoder model, the channel signal is y(t) = A_1 e^{j(ω_1 t+φ_1)} + A_2 e^{j(ω_2 t+φ_2)}. What is the instantaneous amplitude |y(t)|?

- (a) √(A_1^2 + A_2^2 + 2A_1 A_2 cos[(ω_1−ω_2)t + (φ_1−φ_2)])
- (b) A_1 + A_2
- (c) √(A_1^2 + A_2^2)
- (d) |A_1 − A_2| cos[(ω_1−ω_2)t]

Hint 1: Compute |y(t)|^2 = y(t) · y*(t) and use Euler's formula for the cross terms.

Hint 2: The cross terms contribute 2A_1 A_2 cos[difference-frequency · t + difference-phase].

**Answer: (a).** |y(t)|^2 = Re[y]^2 + Im[y]^2. Expanding and using cos identities gives A_1^2 + A_2^2 + 2A_1 A_2 cos[(ω_1−ω_2)t + (φ_1−φ_2)]. The amplitude therefore beats at the difference frequency (ω_1−ω_2), which is the classic interference (beating) pattern between two nearby sinusoids.

#### `sinmodel-vocoder-2` - difficulty 1; concepts: instantaneous-frequency, phase-vocoder, single-sinusoid, limiting-case, sinusoidal-modeling

**Q.** In the two-sinusoid phase-vocoder model y(t) = A_1 e^{j(ω_1 t+φ_1)} + A_2 e^{j(ω_2 t+φ_2)}, the instantaneous frequency is ω(t) = (A_1^2ω_1 + A_2^2ω_2 + A_1 A_2(ω_1+ω_2)cos[(ω_1−ω_2)t+Δφ]) / |y(t)|^2. When A_2→0 this simplifies to what?

- (a) ω_1
- (b) (ω_1 + ω_2) / 2
- (c) ω_2
- (d) 0

Hint 1: Set A_2=0 in both numerator and denominator of the instantaneous-frequency formula.

Hint 2: Every term multiplied by A_2 vanishes.

**Answer: (a).** Setting A_2=0 in both numerator and denominator: numerator becomes A_1^2ω_1; denominator becomes A_1^2. Their ratio is ω_1. This confirms the phase-vocoder is well behaved when a single sinusoid occupies the channel: the instantaneous frequency estimate equals the true sinusoidal frequency.

#### `sinmodel-vocoder-3` - difficulty 2; concepts: resolution, phase-vocoder, two-sinusoid-model, beat-period, parameter-estimation

**Q.** Two sinusoids at frequencies ω_1 and ω_2 are present in a phase-vocoder channel. According to the book's rule of thumb, how long must a rectangular analysis window be to resolve the two frequencies by finding FFT peaks?

- (a) At least two full cycles of the difference frequency: M ≥ 2f_s/Δf
- (b) One full beat period: T = 2π/(ω_1 − ω_2)
- (c) One sample: T = 1/f_s
- (d) Half a beat period: T = π/(ω_1 − ω_2)

Hint 1: The two main lobes of the window transform must be resolved: Δω ≥ 2Ω_M = 4π/M for the rectangular window.

Hint 2: Two full cycles of the difference frequency is the rule of thumb; a finer analysis shows 1.44 cycles can suffice.

**Answer: (a).** Resolving the two window-transform main lobes requires Δω ≥ 2Ω_M for the rectangular window, i.e., M ≥ 2f_s/Δf — the window must span at least two full cycles of the difference frequency. A more detailed study shows that 1.44 cycles of the difference frequency suffices for fully accurate peak-frequency measurement under the rectangular window. In principle (no noise, exactly two ideal sinusoids), arbitrarily small separations can be resolved by methods beyond FFT peak-finding.

## 10.5.1 TSM and S+N+T

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/TSM_S_N_T.html

#### `apps-tsm-snt-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: snt-tsm, transient-handling

**Q.** How does S+N+T handle time-scale modification in transient regions?

- (a) Same as everywhere else
- (b) Transients only translate in time; they don't stretch or squeeze - keeping attacks crisp
- (c) Transients are removed
- (d) TSM is impossible for transients

Hint 1: Transients need to stay sharp.

Hint 2: Elastic regions only outside transient intervals.

**Answer: (b).** Translating transients without scaling them prevents attack 'smearing' under time-stretching. A continuous 'transientness' measure can interpolate between rigid (translate) and elastic (stretch) behavior.

## 10.5.2 TSM by Resampling STFTs Across Time

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/TSM_Resampling_STFTs_Across.html

#### `apps-tsm-stft-1` - difficulty 3; concepts: stft-tsm, phase-vocoder-tsm

**Q.** How does STFT-based TSM by factor α work?

- (a) Resample the audio
- (b) Advance the resynthesis frame pointer by R/α per output hop, interpolating STFT magnitudes between original frames; choose phases for continuity
- (c) Sub-sample the FFT bins
- (d) Change the sampling rate

Hint 1: Stretch the time axis between STFT frames.

Hint 2: Phase vocoder TSM.

**Answer: (b).** WOLA phase-vocoder TSM: input frames are taken at the analysis hop R, output frames are taken from the (interpolated) STFT at hop R/α. The result is α× longer/shorter at the same pitch.

## 10.5 Phase Continuation

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Phase_Continuation.html

#### `apps-phase-cont-1` - difficulty 3; concepts: phase-continuation, phasiness

**Q.** What are the two competing desiderata when interpolating STFT phase across time for TSM?

- (a) Speed and accuracy
- (b) (1) Sinusoids should pick up where they left off across frames; (2) relative phase between bins within a frame should be preserved
- (c) Causality and stability
- (d) Time and frequency resolution

Hint 1: Across-frame continuity vs. within-frame phase relations.

Hint 2: You can't have both in general.

**Answer: (b).** Condition (1) preserves smooth tonal continuation; (2) preserves the time-domain pulse structure within each frame. They generally conflict; transient frames favor (2), stationary frames favor (1).

## 10.5 TSM Examples

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/TSM_Examples.html

#### `tsm-beat-rate-1` - difficulty 1; concepts: time-scale-modification, beats, amplitude-envelope, test-signals

**Q.** The TSM test signal consists of two constant-amplitude sinusoids near 400 Hz. What frequency separation is used to obtain an amplitude envelope with 10 beats per second?

- (a) 10 Hz
- (b) 5 Hz
- (c) 20 Hz
- (d) 400 Hz

Hint 1: The beat rate is set by the difference between the two frequencies.

Hint 2: The text picks the separation to equal the desired beats per second.

**Answer: (a).** Two constant-amplitude sinusoids separated by 10 Hz produce the stated beat rate of 10 beats/sec, which is exactly the reason the text chose that separation: the beating envelope makes it easy to see whether a time-scale-modification algorithm preserves the intra-frame amplitude envelope. 5 Hz (b) and 20 Hz (c) would give different beat rates, and 400 Hz (d) is the center frequency, not the separation.

#### `tsm-frame-rate-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: stft, hop-size, frame-rate, time-scale-modification

**Q.** The vocoder STFT frame size is 45 ms and the analysis hop size is 1/4 frame. What is the resulting analysis frame rate?

- (a) 22 Hz
- (b) 45 Hz
- (c) 89 Hz
- (d) 356 Hz

Hint 1: First convert the hop size to seconds.

Hint 2: Frame rate = 1 / hop size; the hop is 11.25 ms.

**Answer: (c).** A hop of one quarter of 45 ms is 11.25 ms, and 1/0.01125 s = 88.9 ≈ 89 Hz, as stated in the text. 22 Hz (a) is the frame rate you would get with a full-frame (non-overlapping) hop of 45 ms; 45 Hz (b) confuses the frame size in ms with a rate in Hz; 356 Hz (d) is four times too large, as if the hop were 1/16 of a frame.

## 10.5 Phase-Continued STFT TSM

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Phase_Continued_STFT_TSM.html

#### `tsm-phase-continued-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: phase-vocoder, time-scale-modification, phase-coherence, modulation-sidebands

**Q.** In phase-continued STFT time-scale modification, distortion products appear in the output spectrum at multiples of the frame rate. What causes them?

- (a) Aliasing caused by downsampling each filter-bank channel
- (b) Quantization noise in the FFT
- (c) Relative phase is not preserved across FFT bins, so the intra-frame amplitude envelope is distorted and transitions ungracefully into the next frame
- (d) The window transform side lobes leak into neighboring channels

Hint 1: Ask what is periodic at the frame rate in the time-domain output.

Hint 2: Each frame's internal amplitude envelope is wrong and then jumps at the frame boundary.

**Answer: (c).** Because each bin's phase is continued independently, the relative phase across bins is lost; the amplitude envelope within each frame is therefore not preserved, and the resulting frame-rate-periodic distortion shows up as modulation sidebands at multiples of the frame rate. Such frame-rate sidebands are typical of nonlinearly processed STFTs. Channel-downsampling aliasing (a), FFT quantization (b), and side-lobe leakage (d) are unrelated to the frame-rate periodicity of this artifact.

## 10.5 Relative-Phase-Preserving STFT TSM

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Relative_Phase_Preserving_STFT_TSM.html

#### `tsm-phase-locked-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: phase-vocoder, phase-locking, time-scale-modification, spectral-distortion

**Q.** Compared with the phase-continued vocoder, what is the characteristic trade-off of the relative-phase-preserving (“phase-locked”) vocoder at 2× time expansion?

- (a) The amplitude envelope is preserved within each frame, but individual FFT-bin frequencies become phase-modulated from frame to frame
- (b) The bin frequencies are exact, but the beat rate is halved
- (c) Both the envelope and the bin phases are exactly preserved, with no distortion
- (d) The output duration is no longer doubled

Hint 1: Something has to give when relative phase is locked across bins.

Hint 2: The distortion moves from frame-rate sidebands to a broadband character.

**Answer: (a).** Preserving relative phase across bins keeps each frame's amplitude envelope intact and makes frame-to-frame segues look much better at the envelope level, but the price is that the individual bin frequencies get phase-modulated from frame to frame; the resulting spectral distortion is broadband rather than concentrated at multiples of the frame rate. The beat rate is preserved (b is wrong — both plots show the same beats per second), no method is distortion-free (c), and the duration is still doubled as desired (d).

## 10.5 SOLA-FS TSM

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/SOLA_FS_TSM.html

#### `apps-sola-fs-1` - difficulty 3; concepts: sola, transient-stutter

**Q.** What is a known weakness of SOLA-type time-domain TSM algorithms?

- (a) They cannot handle stereo
- (b) They can 'stutter' if attack transients are repeated; transient frames need special handling
- (c) They require an FFT
- (d) They cannot speed up signals

Hint 1: Repeated transients = double attack.

Hint 2: Cross-correlation alignment doesn't avoid the duplication.

**Answer: (b).** SOLA achieves slow-down by repeating frames at maximum local cross-correlation. If a transient frame is repeated, the attack is heard twice - a stutter. Detect transients and only stretch in steady-state regions.

## 10.6 Gaussian Windowed Chirps (Chirplets)

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Gaussian_Windowed_Chirps_Chirplets.html

#### `apps-chirplet-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: chirplet, gaussian-chirp

**Q.** What is a chirplet?

- (a) A sinusoid
- (b) A Gaussian-windowed chirp: e^(-(α-jβ)t^2) - amplitude Gaussian with quadratic (frequency-sweeping) phase
- (c) A short impulse
- (d) A wavelet

Hint 1: Real part of -p·t^2 is Gaussian; imaginary is quadratic phase.

Hint 2: Both time and frequency representations are Gaussian-shaped.

**Answer: (b).** Combining Gaussian decay (real part of -p t^2) with quadratic phase (imaginary part) gives a Gaussian-windowed chirp. Its Fourier transform is also Gaussian - a self-dual generalization of the Gabor atom.

## 10.6.1 Chirplet Fourier Transform

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Chirplet_Fourier_Transform.html

#### `chirplet-ft-complexp-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: gaussian, chirplet, fourier-transform, convergence

**Q.** The Fourier pair e^(−pt^2) ↔ √(π/p) e^(−ω^2/4p) is valid for which values of the parameter p?

- (a) Only real positive p
- (b) Only purely imaginary p
- (c) All complex p with Re{p} > 0
- (d) All complex p except p = 0

Hint 1: What is needed for e^(−pt^2) to decay as |t| grows?

Hint 2: A condition on the real part of p.

**Answer: (c).** The result holds for any complex p whose real part is positive; a positive real part is what makes e^(−pt^2) decay (and hence the integral converge) as |t| → ∞. Restricting to real p (a) would exclude chirplets entirely; purely imaginary p (b) gives no Gaussian decay at all; and (d) admits values such as Re{p} < 0 for which the integral diverges.

#### `chirplet-zero-freq-t0-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: chirplet, instantaneous-frequency, signal-modeling, gaussian

**Q.** Writing p = α − jβ gives x(t) = e^(−αt^2) e^(jβt^2), a Gaussian-windowed chirp. Why does the text add an arbitrary frequency offset before using this as a signal model?

- (a) Because the Gaussian envelope is not centered at t = 0
- (b) Because the chirp's oscillation frequency is zero at t = 0, whereas a real signal component generally has some nonzero frequency there
- (c) Because the Fourier transform would otherwise be complex
- (d) Because β must be positive for the transform to exist

Hint 1: Differentiate the phase βt^2 to get instantaneous frequency.

Hint 2: At t = 0 the instantaneous frequency 2βt is zero.

**Answer: (b).** The instantaneous phase is βt^2, whose derivative 2βt vanishes at t = 0; the chirp therefore always sweeps through zero frequency at the window center. Adding a frequency offset lets the model represent a component at any center frequency. The Gaussian is centered at t = 0 (a); the transform of a complex chirplet is complex either way (c); and β may be positive or negative — only Re{p} = α > 0 is required (d).

## 10.6 Modulated Gaussian-Windowed Chirp

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Modulated_Gaussian_Windowed_Chirp.html

#### `chirplet-modulation-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: modulation-theorem, chirplet, gaussian, frequency-shift

**Q.** Applying the modulation theorem x(t)e^(−jω_0 t) ↔ X(ω+ω_0) to the complex-Gaussian pair gives which transform for e^(−pt^2) e^(−jω_0 t)?

- (a) √(π/p) e^(−(ω−ω_0)^2/4p)
- (b) √(π/p) e^(−(ω+ω_0)^2/4p)
- (c) √(π/p) e^(−ω^2/4p) · e^(−jω_0ω)
- (d) √(π/(p+jω_0)) e^(−ω^2/4p)

Hint 1: Modulation in time is a shift in frequency — substitute the shifted argument.

Hint 2: Replace ω by ω+ω_0 everywhere it appears in the transform.

**Answer: (b).** Multiplying by e^(−jω_0 t) replaces ω by ω+ω_0 in the transform, giving √(π/p)e^(−(ω+ω_0)^2/4p). Option (a) has the sign of the shift reversed (that would correspond to multiplying by e^(+jω_0 t)); (c) applies the shift theorem (a time delay) instead of its dual; (d) incorrectly modifies the Gaussian parameter p.

## 10.6.3 Identifying Chirp Rate

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Identifying_Chirp_Rate.html

#### `apps-chirp-rate-1` - difficulty 3; concepts: chirp-rate-estimation, phase-curvature

**Q.** How can chirp rate β be estimated from the spectrum of a Gaussian-windowed chirp?

- (a) From phase curvature: c_p = d^2(angle F)/dω^2 - both log-magnitude and phase are parabolas, parabolic interpolation gives both α and β
- (b) By taking another FFT
- (c) It cannot be estimated
- (d) By autocorrelation

Hint 1: Parabolic phase = chirp.

Hint 2: Curvature of phase recovers β.

**Answer: (a).** Both log|F(ω)| and arg F(ω) are parabolas in ω (involving α and β respectively). Curvatures c_m and c_p at the spectral peak give both window-rate and chirp-rate estimates.

## 10.6.3 Chirplet Frequency-Rate Estimation

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Chirplet_Frequency_Rate_Estimation.html

#### `chirplet-beta-estimate-1` - difficulty 3; concepts: chirplet, chirp-rate-estimation, spectral-peak, parabolic-interpolation

**Q.** Given the measured window curvature α̂ and weighted-average measured curvatures [c_m] and [c_p] along the log-magnitude and phase of a spectral peak, the chirp-rate estimate is

- (a) β̂ = α̂ [c_m] [c_p]
- (b) β̂ = α̂ [c_m] / [c_p]
- (c) β̂ = α̂ [c_p] / [c_m]
- (d) β̂ = [c_p] / (α̂ [c_m])

Hint 1: The chirp rate β is tied to the curvature of the phase, and α to the curvature of the log magnitude.

Hint 2: The ratio of phase curvature to log-magnitude curvature equals β/α.

**Answer: (c).** Since c_m = −α/[2(α^2+β^2)] and c_p = −β/[2(α^2+β^2)], the common factor cancels in the ratio and c_p/c_m = β/α, giving β̂ = α̂[c_p]/[c_m] as boxed in the text. Option (b) inverts the ratio; (a) multiplies rather than divides; (d) misplaces α̂.

## 10.6.3 Simulation Results

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Simulation_Results.html

#### `chirplet-sim-downgoing-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: chirplet, chirp-rate, unwrapped-phase, parabolic-fit

**Q.** In the simulation, a Gaussian-windowed chirp whose frequency decreases from 1 kHz to 500 Hz is analyzed. Compared with an upgoing chirp, what changes in the spectrum near the peak?

- (a) The log-magnitude becomes a straight line instead of a parabola
- (b) The curvature of the unwrapped phase changes sign
- (c) The peak magnitude doubles
- (d) The unwrapped phase becomes constant

Hint 1: Which of the two parabolic fits carries the sign of the chirp rate?

Hint 2: Log magnitude tracks α; unwrapped phase tracks β, and β reverses sign.

**Answer: (b).** The unwrapped-phase curvature at the peak is proportional to the chirp rate β, which is negative for a downgoing chirp and positive for an upgoing one; hence the phase parabola flips its concavity. The log-magnitude parabola is governed by α (always positive), so it does not straighten (a) or otherwise flip; peak magnitude (c) and a constant phase (d) are not implied.

#### `chirplet-sim-truncation-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: chirplet, gaussian-window, truncation, parabolic-fit

**Q.** In the chirplet simulation, the parabolic fits to the dB magnitude and unwrapped phase are good but not exact. What does the text give as the reason?

- (a) The FFT length is too short
- (b) The chirp rate is too high for the Gaussian model
- (c) The signal is truncated in the time domain; without truncation the parabolic fits would be perfect
- (d) The phase was unwrapped incorrectly

Hint 1: An ideal Gaussian has infinite support.

Hint 2: The text says the fits would be perfect if the signal were not truncated in time.

**Answer: (c).** An ideal (untruncated) Gaussian-windowed chirp has exactly parabolic log-magnitude and unwrapped phase spectra. The simulated signal is finite in length, so the Gaussian is truncated and the fits become approximate; the text notes explicitly that without time-domain truncation the fits would be perfect. It also observes that phase modeling is most accurate where the magnitude is substantial — not that the unwrapping is wrong (d). FFT length (a) and chirp rate (b) are not the stated cause.

## 10.7 FFT Filter Banks

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/FFT_Filter_Banks.html

#### `apps-fft-fb-1` - difficulty 1; concepts: fft-filter-banks

**Q.** What kind of filter banks are addressed in this STFT-based 'FFT Filter Banks' section?

- (a) Critically sampled compression-oriented banks
- (b) Non-compression filter banks where each channel doesn't have to be critically sampled - simpler designs based on STFT methodology
- (c) Wavelet only
- (d) Analog filter banks

Hint 1: Non-compression context.

Hint 2: Avoids the strictness of perfect-reconstruction critically-sampled designs.

**Answer: (b).** Outside compression we needn't critically sample. The chapter develops simple, robust nonuniform filter banks (with arbitrarily small reconstruction error) by smoothing/grouping FFT bins.

## 10.7 Audio Filter Banks

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Audio_Filter_Banks.html

#### `apps-audio-fb-1` - difficulty 1; concepts: auditory-filter-bank, constant-q

**Q.** Why must auditory filter banks be nonuniform?

- (a) FFT requires it
- (b) Frequency resolution of human hearing decreases (channel bandwidths increase) with frequency
- (c) It is a coincidence
- (d) They are not

Hint 1: Constant-Q is roughly auditory.

Hint 2: Linear at low f, exponential at high f.

**Answer: (b).** Critical bandwidths grow with frequency, so any approximation of the ear's filter bank must have wider bands at higher frequencies - a nonuniform (often constant-Q) bank.

## 10.7.2 Basic Idea

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Basic_Idea.html

#### `nonuniform-fb-basic-idea-1` - difficulty 1; concepts: nonuniform-filter-bank, octave-filter-bank, inverse-fft, downsampling

**Q.** What is the basic idea behind the FFT-based nonuniform (e.g., octave) filter bank introduced here?

- (a) Apply a different window length to each FFT frame
- (b) Partition the FFT bins into the desired nonuniform bands and perform a smaller inverse FFT on each band to obtain a downsampled time-domain signal for that band
- (c) Compute one FFT per octave and discard the rest of the spectrum
- (d) Use a bank of IIR bandpass filters whose coefficients are derived from the FFT

Hint 1: Think about how many bins each band contains, and what a smaller inverse FFT produces.

Hint 2: Group the bins, then inverse-FFT each group separately.

**Answer: (b).** Bins of one large FFT are grouped into the desired (nonuniform) bands, and a smaller inverse FFT per group synthesizes a time-domain signal for that band; because each group has fewer bins than the full FFT, that band signal is naturally downsampled. In the simple length-8 example, successive frames are non-overlapping (rectangular window advancing its full length). Options (a), (c), and (d) describe different schemes not used here.

## 10.7.3 Summing STFT Bins

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Summing_STFT_Bins.html

#### `apps-sum-bins-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: bin-grouping, hop-size-constraint

**Q.** What constrains the maximum STFT hop size when adjacent FFT bins are summed to make a wider band?

- (a) FFT length
- (b) The widest pass-band in the resulting filter bank - higher bandwidth requires faster time sampling
- (c) Sample rate
- (d) Window length only

Hint 1: Wider passband → higher Nyquist rate.

Hint 2: Hop size capped by the broadest channel.

**Answer: (b).** Widening a band requires more samples per second to avoid aliasing. The widest band (e.g., the top octave) sets the maximum hop size; lower-frequency channels are then heavily oversampled.

## 10.7.4 Inverse Transforming STFT Bin Groups

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Inverse_Transforming_STFT_Bin.html

#### `apps-ifft-bin-1` - difficulty 3; concepts: band-ifft, critical-sampling

**Q.** How can N_k-wide bands of the STFT be efficiently converted to critically downsampled time-domain samples?

- (a) Take the IFFT of just the N_k bins of the band - produces N_k critically-sampled time-domain samples per frame
- (b) Use a separate FIR filter
- (c) Wavelet transform
- (d) Goertzel algorithm

Hint 1: DFT length = effective downsampling factor.

Hint 2: Use the aliasing theorem.

**Answer: (a).** By the aliasing theorem, the length-N_k IFFT of the in-band spectrum equals the N_k-fold downsampled full-rate IFFT - a direct, efficient critical sampling.

## 10.7.5 Improving the Channel Filters

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Improving_Channel_Filters.html

#### `apps-improve-ch-1` - difficulty 3; concepts: channel-stop-band, window-choice

**Q.** Why does using a Dolph-Chebyshev FFT analysis window dramatically improve channel-filter stop-band rejection compared to the rectangular window?

- (a) It reduces noise
- (b) Channel-filter stop-bands are sums of FFT-window side lobes; lower side lobes → lower stop-band gain
- (c) It is faster
- (d) It is real-valued

Hint 1: Channel response is a sum of window-transform shifts.

Hint 2: Window controls side-lobe level.

**Answer: (b).** Each FFT bin's response is a shifted FFT-window transform. Summing N_k adjacent shifts produces a channel filter whose stop-band is a sum of side lobes - lower side lobes (better window) directly improves stop-band rejection.

## 10.7.6 Fast Octave Filter Banks

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Fast_Octave_Filter_Banks.html

#### `apps-fast-oct-1` - difficulty 3; concepts: real-signal-spectrum, octave-partition

**Q.** Why is straightforward octave-band partitioning of a real-signal spectrum problematic?

- (a) Real signals have no spectrum
- (b) The number of unique spectral samples for a length-N FFT (real input) is N/2+1, which is not a power of 2 - so octave bands of power-of-2 widths don't pack cleanly
- (c) The FFT cannot be inverted
- (d) Octave filter banks are always nonlinear

Hint 1: Conjugate symmetry leaves an awkward sample count.

Hint 2: Half-bin shift removes dc and Nyquist.

**Answer: (b).** DC and Nyquist samples have no conjugate counterparts, breaking the power-of-2 packing. Solutions include the half-bin spectral-rotation trick (next subsection) or extending bands to overlap.

## 10.7.7 Spectral Rotation of Real Signals

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Spectral_Rotation_Real_Signals.html

#### `apps-spec-rot-1` - difficulty 3; concepts: spectral-rotation, real-signal-octave

**Q.** What does multiplying a real signal by exp(-jπn/N) before FFT achieve?

- (a) Doubles the spectrum
- (b) Half-bin spectral rotation: gives N/2 positive- and N/2 negative-frequency samples with no dc or Nyquist sample - power-of-2 octave packing per half
- (c) Removes negative frequencies
- (d) Gibbs cancellation

Hint 1: Phase factor by half a bin.

Hint 2: Removes the awkward dc and Nyquist points.

**Answer: (b).** The half-bin shift moves all spectral samples off dc and the Nyquist limit. Both positive- and negative-frequency halves end up with N/2 samples each - allowing a clean octave partition with power-of-2 sub-IFFTs.

## 10.7.8 Improving the Octave Band Filters

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Improving_Octave_Band_Filters.html

#### `apps-improve-oct-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: octave-filter-bank, chebyshev-window

**Q.** When upgrading the rectangular-window octave filter bank to a Dolph-Chebyshev (chebwin(127,80)) version, what changes about the filter-bank guarantees?

- (a) Stop-band rejection improves to ~80 dB while perfect reconstruction (full-rate) still holds
- (b) Reconstruction breaks completely
- (c) Aliasing is eliminated
- (d) The bank becomes single-band

Hint 1: PR is preserved at the full rate.

Hint 2: Stop-band performance set by window's side lobes.

**Answer: (a).** Full-rate PR depends on the underlying STFT being PR and channel filters summing to a constant in frequency - both still true. Stop-band rejection now follows the Dolph-Chebyshev side-lobe spec (~80 dB), much better than the rectangular case.

## 10.7.9 Aliasing on Downsampling

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Aliasing_Downsampling.html

#### `apps-alias-down-1` - difficulty 3; concepts: downsampling-aliasing, crossover

**Q.** When the chebwin-based octave bank is critically downsampled, where does residual aliasing concentrate?

- (a) At dc
- (b) In the transition bands - which are aliased about their midpoints (folding frequencies at band crossovers)
- (c) Only at Nyquist
- (d) Nowhere

Hint 1: Folding occurs at band-edge midpoints.

Hint 2: Transition aliasing dominates the residual error.

**Answer: (b).** Critical sampling places folding frequencies at the channel crossovers. Transition bands fold onto themselves, producing audible aliasing in critically sampled designs unless transitions are tucked into a wider IFFT band.

## 10.7.10 Restricting Aliasing to Stop-Bands

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Restricting_Aliasing_Stop_Bands.html

#### `apps-restrict-1` - difficulty 3; concepts: band-extension, stop-band-aliasing

**Q.** How can aliasing be restricted to stop-band energy in the FFT octave filter bank?

- (a) Wider IFFTs that enclose each band PLUS its two transition bands - keeping the IFFT length a power of 2 and folding only stop-band energy
- (b) Rectangular window
- (c) Increase sampling rate
- (d) Add more channels

Hint 1: Make IFFT bands wider to enclose transitions.

Hint 2: Stop-band energy is small to begin with.

**Answer: (a).** By extending each IFFT to also cover both transition regions, only stop-band energy aliases. The aliased stop-band energy is bounded by the channel-filter stop-band rejection - essentially negligible in practice.

## 10.7.10 Tightening the IFFTs

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Tightening_IFFTs.html

#### `apps-tighten-1` - difficulty 3; concepts: quasi-octave, tight-ifft

**Q.** How can the 'quasi octave' filter bank be made nearly as efficient as the heavily aliased version?

- (a) Eliminate transitions
- (b) Narrow each pass-band by twice the transition width, so the enclosed band+transitions still fit into the original power-of-2 IFFT length
- (c) Use a larger FFT
- (d) Switch to wavelets

Hint 1: Move some 'octave width' to the transition regions.

Hint 2: Keeps the IFFT lengths short.

**Answer: (b).** Octave-bands shrunk by 2×(transition width) leave room for the transitions inside the same power-of-2 IFFT. The bands are slightly less than one octave wide, hence 'quasi-octave.'

## 10.7 Real Filter Bank Example

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Real_Filter_Bank_Example.html

#### `nonuniform-fb-real-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: octave-filter-bank, conjugate-symmetry, real-signals, band-allocation

**Q.** How is the octave filter bank adapted for real input signals?

- (a) The FFT size must be doubled
- (b) A Hilbert transform is applied to each band
- (c) Bands are allocated between dc and half the sampling rate, and conjugate symmetry automatically supplies the bands above half the sampling rate, so the band-allocation algorithm itself needs no modification
- (d) Each band must be modulated down to dc before the inverse FFT

Hint 1: What special property does the spectrum of a real signal have?

Hint 2: Conjugate symmetry means the upper half of the spectrum is determined by the lower half.

**Answer: (c).** For real signals the spectrum is conjugate symmetric, so only the bands between dc and f_s/2 need be allocated; the corresponding bands in the upper half-spectrum are constructed automatically by conjugate symmetry. Consequently the band-allocation algorithm is unchanged from the complex-signal case. Doubling the FFT (a), Hilbert transforming (b), and heterodyning each band (d) are not required.

## 10.7 Optimal Band Filters

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Optimal_Band_Filters.html

#### `apps-opt-bands-1` - difficulty 3; concepts: dolph-chebyshev-prototype, filter-bank-optimality

**Q.** Why is the Dolph-Chebyshev window often a near-optimal choice for the FFT-filter-bank lowpass prototype, even though it's only Chebyshev-optimal for one-bin pass-bands?

- (a) It uses fewer multiplies
- (b) Summing window-transform shifts to make wider channels generally improves the stop-band rejection beyond the prototype's spec, satisfying the Chebyshev optimality of the bank as a whole
- (c) It is the only valid choice
- (d) It avoids zero-padding

Hint 1: Wider sums of side lobes can only reduce, not increase, stop-band level.

Hint 2: Worst-case channel is the narrowest one.

**Answer: (b).** Wider channels are made by superposing shifted prototypes. Their summed stop-band is no worse (typically better) than the prototype's, so the worst-case channel determines the bank's rejection. The minimum-bandwidth channel is exactly Chebyshev-optimal.

## 10 FFT Filter-Bank Summary and Fourier Duality with OLA

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/FFT_Filter_Bank_Summary_Fourier.html

#### `apps-fb-summary-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: ola-fbs-duality

**Q.** How is the FFT filter-bank approach the Fourier dual of OLA STFT processing?

- (a) OLA decomposes time into overlapping frames; FFT filter banks decompose frequency into overlapping bands. Both pad to the next power of 2 and IFFT/FFT efficiently
- (b) They are identical
- (c) They are unrelated
- (d) FFT filter banks don't use the FFT

Hint 1: OLA in time ↔ band-add in frequency.

Hint 2: Same architecture, opposite domain.

**Answer: (a).** Time-domain overlap-add (OLA) corresponds to frequency-domain band overlap-add. Pad-to-power-of-2 in time = pad-to-power-of-2 in frequency. The methods are complete duals.
